results.content: We tested Open Claw, Hermes Agent, and Prime Agent on simple puzzles that keep returning overtime. To our surprise, none of them learned wipe their memory before every puzzle, and they do just as well. They can't even beat a simple baseline, and they don't get better at solving new puzzles either. But a small model trained to drive its harness both gets better at puzzles it has seen and also learns to solve new ones. Introducing continual arc. How well does your agent really learn? We ran all three harnesses on the same model, GPT 6 Lunar at low, medium, and high. Reasoning effort each as it ships with its memory switched on. Continual arc builds on Francois Chollet's arc. Each puzzle hides a rule you work out from a few examples here. Every protruding corner shoots a line to the edge. [...] To learn a puzzle, a harness has to store its rule, then find it again. The three harnesses failed for different reasons. At every reasoning effort we tested, Prime Agent never stored anything for later, only what it marks. Global outlives a session, as its instructions told it, and in 600 sessions it never marked a thing in its words. There's no need for a persistent harness, since it's just one instance. Hermes agent did store skills and opened one on nearly every return, but they were general tips on solving puzzles, hardly ever the rule of the one in front of it, so it paid for the same examples again. Open Claw kept every conversation, but its agent rarely went back to look, and its dreams only keep what the agent keeps looking. UO they kept nothing. Then we ran them again, this time [...] clients' accounts is quicker with a new client too, because they've gotten better at accounting 𝘪𝘯 𝘨𝘦𝘯𝘦𝘳𝘢𝘭. We couldn't find a benchmark that measures memorization and generalization separately, so we built one. Continual-ARC is a long stream of ARC puzzles. The same puzzles recur with fresh inputs while new ones arrive, so an agent can't just reuse an answer it remembers. Each visit to a puzzle has a budget of 16: every worked example the agent asks for costs one, every wrong answer costs one, and a visit the agent fails costs the full 16. We score learning by how much less of that budget an agent spends than the same agent with its memory wiped. results.title: Continual-ARC: Do Agent Harnesses Learn From Experience? | CellCog
results.content:
A paper posted on November 10, 2026 tested whether three agent harnesses get cheaper at puzzles they have already solved, and found that as shipped none of them did. Its author, Daniel Lenton of Unify, summed it up on X as OpenClaw, Hermes Agent and Prime Agent not learning from experience. The paper’s own tables say something narrower than that sentence, and they carry a second result that got less attention.

This post is read from the paper on arXiv, Unify’s blog post about it, Lenton’s thread on X and the benchmark’s GitHub page. We read the sections and tables named below, not all 51 pages, and we ran nothing ourselves.

### On this page · 10 sectionsOpen [...] ### Q1Do OpenClaw and Hermes Agent learn from experience?

On this one benchmark, as shipped and on GPT-6 Luna, the paper measured no saving from their memory. Given explicit instructions on what to store, both saved a large share on puzzles they had met. Neither gained on new puzzles once the paper’s correction is applied.

### Q2Who wrote the Continual-ARC paper?

Daniel Lenton of Unify is the only author. It was submitted to arXiv on November 10, 2026 and runs to 51 pages.

### Q3Which versions were tested?

The paper’s reference list gives Hermes Agent 0.20.2 and OpenClaw 2026.9.5, both accessed in September 2026. The model was GPT-6 Luna at low, medium and high reasoning effort.

### Q4Does the result apply to stronger models? [...] ## § 04Why they saved nothing, per the paper#

- Prime Agent never marked a lesson as global in 600 sessions, so every session opened on the line “No saved harness entries yet”.
- Hermes Agent opened a skill on 524 of 525 returns, per Lenton’s thread, but the skills held general tips.
- OpenClaw, when asked to save, wrote 47 to 84 notes per run and read the one named for the puzzle on at most 1 percent of returning visits.
- The paper’s reading. It writes: “This suggests that the harnesses’ own prompting is not well suited to this domain”.

results.content: A returning task is solved at cost 0, with no demonstration and the first answer right, almost only by a learner that uses something it kept about the task. On the stream’s cells, whose stores we read, the stateless methods never do so, and method H on at most one of a cell’s 175 returning instances, while H-A does so on 18, 31 and 47% at low, medium and high effort for prime-agent, 15, 41 and 38 for hermes-agent, and on none for openclaw. H-E does so on 46 to 80% for every harness, and PL on 72 to 86. openclaw did store when asked: its H-A cells wrote 47, 59 and 84 notes at low, medium and high effort, 40, 39 and 50 of them named for a task. What it lacks is a path back. It loads only its MEMORY.md at the start of a session, wrote none, and read a note named for the task on none of the [...] Appendix E). prime-agent kept an entry for later sessions only when the agent saved it as global, as its prompt explained, and the agent never did. hermes-agent loaded its skills on every return, but they held general advice which did not affect spend. openclaw never promoted a memory at all, and an earlier correct answer never came back on any of its returns. None of the three harnesses kept the demonstrations it paid for, each buying 2.3 to 3.9 pairs per instance where the demo-cache floor bought 1.4 to 2.6. This suggests that the harnesses’ own prompting is not well suited to this domain. [...] openclaw keeps one conversation for its agent, in which each of our instances opens with a reset, in a database searchable by text. Dreaming, openclaw’s scheduled consolidation, ran every hour of the stream and never promoted a memory into MEMORY.md, which every later session reads: its gate needs three recall signals and three distinct queries from the agent’s own memory searches, and no entry of its short-term store had more than two signals or a recall by the agent. The skill workshop wrote three skills in the low-effort cell and none at medium and high effort. results.title: Why we built Continual-ARC. · unify
results.content:
Agent harnesses such as OpenClaw[\[1\]](#ref-1), Hermes Agent[\[2\]](#ref-2) and Prime Agent[\[3\]](#ref-3) keep notes and write themselves skills, and they're often described as a way for an agent to keep learning on the job. We wanted to know what kind of learning that is, and to put it on the same scale as training the model's weights as it works, but couldn't find a benchmark that would let us.

Learning on the job can mean two things. Someone who has done the same client's quarterly accounts four times is quicker the fifth time, because they remember how that client's books work. Someone who has done a hundred clients' accounts is quicker with a new client too, because they've got better at accounts. The first is memory, and the second is the learning we care about most. [...] A harness could still prove us wrong, most likely one that refactors what it keeps into small functions it can reuse. Re-ARC writes all 400 training rules from one library of 160 primitive functions, and program synthesis has learned libraries like that before[\[15\]](#ref-15)[\[19\]](#ref-19).

## What carries over to real harnesses

Office work has no task ids to file programs by, but we think three lessons from ARC still hold for any harness.

- Store liberally, the examples paid for included, and prune later.
- Store functions, not just notes, checked against the examples kept.
- Bring back what's stored without being asked, by what the current work looks like, which OpenClaw didn't. [...] ## The same in three harnesses on GPT-6 Luna

We also ran Prime Agent, Hermes Agent and OpenClaw on GPT-6 Luna at three reasoning efforts, in case this was Prime Agent's alone. As shipped, none saved a measurable share on the stream, and at high effort not one of their solves after round 100 was free. Prime Agent never marked a lesson global in 600 sessions, and every session opened on "No saved harness entries yet." OpenClaw, asked to save, wrote 47 to 84 notes per run and read one named for the puzzle on at most 1 percent of the returning visits its log kept. (Even Leonard in Memento read his tattoos.) Told the library's procedure, keeping one Python file per puzzle to run first when it returns, every harness saved a measurable share at every effort, 0.17 to 0.62.
